strings.AAC_CountryInfo_Content_desc.1: Antarctica is a cold and unforgiving place. Until the 1950s, the world's southernmost continent was largely ignored, only visited by the occasional scientific research team or the one-off military expedition. The land was divided and claimed by the various powers of the world, but those claims carried little diplomatic weight, as nations preferred to focus on the more inhabitable regions of the world. This would all change in the early 50s, with the Scramble for Antarctica.
strings.AAC_CountryInfo_Content_desc.2: It started with a diplomatic dispute between Chile and Argentina, over a bunch of tiny islands that had formerly been claimed by the British, before their defeat in the Second World War. Both nations, technically, had valid claims to the islands. Argentina, in order to secure their sovereignty over the region they had claimed, began the process to formalize their Antarctica Territory, as well as adopt some of that land that had previously been claimed by the British, and was now left unadministered. Chile contested this action, prompting the United States of America to get involved in their negotiations to help mediate their dispute, as well as stake their own claims to the Antarctic region. Things developed quickly from there.
strings.AAC_CountryInfo_Content_desc.3: The Empire of Japan, eager to further tighten their grip over the Pacific, claimed the area formerly known as Marie Byrd Land, dispatching a small military force in order to secure the territory before the Americans could try anything. The United States of America was quick to respond in kind, consolidating the Australian, New Zealand, and former French claims into the OFN Antarctic Administration. The German Reich usurped the claim of the now-Reichskommissariat Norway, which already overlapped with their Antarctic claim, combining the two into the territory now known as Neuschwabenland. In the hastily finished negotiations between the two South American countries, Chile got the short end of the stick, getting relatively little of their claimed region, while Argentina secured sovereignty over the Trinity Peninsula and many of the surrounding islands. In the span of a week, the Scramble for Antarctica had carved the continent into five territories, as the Cold War grew ever colder.
strings.AAC_CountryInfo_Content_desc.4: By 1962, Antarctica has only become more exploited and militarized. The OFN Antarctic Administration is an important training ground and staging base for clandestine actions in the Indian Ocean, with the Japanese Antarctic Sector doing much of the same to their East. Following some failed colonization attempts in the 1950s, Neuschwabenland has become a testing site for experimental aircraft, cold weather equipment, and, according to unconfirmed reports, nuclear technology. Silently, the Ahnenerbe operate a base out of western Neuschwabenland, conducting their own shadowy operations away from prying eyes. Argentina struggles internally as the Argentinean Navy and Argentinean Antarctic Institute vie for control of the territory, while Chile would enjoy being given a bit more of the swath of territory that they claimed. Even with modern technology, Antarctic is still a dangerous place, ripe with unforgiving weather, deadly crevasses, and poor infrastructure. Try as they may to dominate Antarctica, the frozen continent has never been kind to strangers.
strings.AAC_CountryInfo_Content_desc.5: In the aftermath of World War II, the fascist Axis-aligned government in Argentina sought to take advantage of the new geopolitical reality, beginning an aggressive flag-raising campaign in the Antarctic. Chile deployed her own forces to the region with a reckless abandon that threatened to draw the two nations almost to the brink of war. But what in previous years may have been a mere border dispute began to take on a new global dimension. Increasingly concerned with the threat of an Axis-aligned power in the Southern Cone, US President Dwight Eisenhower in 1950 initiated a series of negotiations to bring together a bloc of South American nations and contain this rising threat. The governments of Brazil, Chile, and Uruguay put aside their differences to sign the Philadelphia Accords, a defense treaty that would ensure any Argentine aggression against one nation would be met with a tripartite response and backing from the US. Not to be outdone, Argentina's new strongman leader, Juan Domingo Perón, received formal recognition of Argentine claims from the Reich.
strings.AAC_CountryInfo_Content_desc.6:
These developments did little to hinder the growing tensions in the far south, however, and in 1952 the continent would experience its first shooting confrontation, however limited, when Chilean surveyors were fired upon by Argentine naval personnel.

Despite their posturing, the superpowers were not looking for a third global conflagration and set about finding a diplomatic resolution to the situation while asserting their own claims over this new arena of international intrigue.

Though the immediate threat of war came to an end, Chile and Argentina found themselves unable to find a permanent diplomatic solution to their disputes, leaving a spectre to hang over the Antarctic wastes.
strings.AAC_CountryInfo_Content_desc.7: This diplomatic procrastination would bear bloody fruit in 1958 when the Argentine Navy launched a series of rogue incursions into Chilean territory, triggered by a skirmish over the obscure Snipe islet whose name would soon become infamous. The Snipe War caught the Chileans completely off guard, and despite a stalwart defense by the soon-to-be national hero Captain José Toribio Merino following a mutiny in port of Valparaíso against the government inaction, the Chilean territory was overrun. The Philadelphia Accords proved themselves to be worth little more than the paper they were signed on as Brazil and Uruguay fumbled for excuses to leave their ally in the lurch. The Argentine government, for its part, scurried to find a way to end the war and preserve its international reputation while appeasing the hawks in the military. After several months of sporadic fighting, an unofficial truce was declared, and the Chilean territories were left shattered; everywhere Argentine jackboots marched across Chilean territory with only isolated holdouts remaining.
strings.AAC_CountryInfo_Content_desc.8:
But not all have given up the dream of restoring Chilean Antarctica to its god given place in the sun. Professor Julio Escudero Guzmán, the newly appointed lead administrator, plots from his base in Arturo Prat to revive the Institute's fortunes. On one hand, he has appointed his close confidant and Socialist Party member Carlos Jaksic to get the territory's finances in order and reorganize what little the Argentines have left them with, and on the other has commissioned the veteran diplomats Marcial Mora Miranda and Enrique Gajardo Villarroel to launch a diplomatic blitz across the Organization of American States to increase international recognition of Chile's Antarctic claims, bringing the might of the free world to bear against their foes.

Meanwhile, Captain Merino, the hero of Snipe, has been placed in charge of the territory's defenses, while he plots the moment to take his final revenge against the Argentine interlopers and the cowards and traitors who he believes aided them.
strings.AAC_THENEWORDER_DESC:
The history of Chile's activity in Antarctica begins in the early twentieth century with the establishment of a small port on the South Shetland Islands for sealers and whalers. Unfortunately for the Chilean government, the British plastered a claim to Antarctica directly across where the Chilean claim would lie decades later.

Despite formally staking their claim three years prior to the Argentineans, the Scramble for Antarctica ended with the Argentineans getting the majority of the British claim, thanks to the hastily conducted negotiations. The Chileans lost even more territory in the aftermath of the Snipe War, with Argentina seizing the disputed territory between the two. The current head of the Chilean Antarctic Territory, Julio Escudero Guzmán, fought to enforce the Chilean claim both before and during the Scramble for Antarctica, and has no plans to stop until Chile's rightful Antarctic territory is restored.
strings.AAC_ending_tt:
...and so ends the starter dish of Best Served Cold. Thank you for playing! We hope you enjoyed your meal.

Stay warm!
 - The Antarctica Team
strings.AAC_Marcial_Mora_Miranda_hog_desc:
Head of Government
Liberal Radicalism
--------------
Marcial Mora Miranda began his long career in politics in the early 1930s, moving between several ministerial positions. He served as ambassador to the United States following the Second World War, and maintained diplomatic relations with Germany, despite his strong opposition to authoritarianism. Additionally, he worked alongside Guzmán to formalize Chile's claims to the Antarctic in the 1940s, which would unfortunately prove to be a fruitless effort when it came time to enforce said claims. Now, as his time in politics has come to a close, the aging statesman is yet again working alongside Guzmán and Villarroel as they diplomatically wrestle for control of Antarctica.
--------------






 £GFX_AAC_Marcial_Mora_Miranda_large
strings.AAC_Enrique_Gajardo_Villarroel_for_desc:
Foreign Minister
Market Liberalism
--------------
After studying at the University of Paris in the late 1920s, Enrique Gajardo Villarroel turned to diplomacy, instead of focusing on the southernmost continent like the other members of the current Antarctic administration. During his career as an ambassador, Villarroel shook many hands and made many connections in Southern and Latin America, from Mexico to Haiti to Uruguay. When the initial Antarctic negotiations between Chile and Argentina began, Villarroel was chosen as part of the delegation, along with Guzmán and Miranda, to secure Chile's rightful territory in the south. The negotiations, clearly, did not go in their favor, and Villarroel has continued his work with the other members of the delegation, putting his connections and ambassadorial skills to work yet again.
--------------






 £GFX_AAC_Enrique_Gajardo_Villarroel_large
strings.AAC_Carlos_Gonzalez_Jaksic_eco_desc:
Economy Minister
Reformist Socialism
--------------
What led up and coming Carlos González Jaksic to the Antarctic coast? One could suggest his graduation as accountant general in Punta Arenas and years as a professor made him a trusty hand to write the budget. Or his service in the Socialist Party's local major offices sold him as a good fit for Guzmán's call for solidarity across the political aisle in Antarctica.

Undoubtedly, his position in the Punta Arenas municipal council makes him a well-connected local ally for the administration. His enemies still whisper about Marxist infiltration. Others see a man who came to politics to represent those he has lived amongst. All see the difficulty of his task: making Chile's slice of Antarctica halfway profitable by decade's end. Before that, Jaksic remembers soberly, he has to scrounge up enough money for them to last a year...
--------------






 £GFX_AAC_Carlos_Gonzalez_Jaksic_large
strings.AAC_Anibal_Pinto_Santa_Cruz_eco_desc:
Economy Minister
Reformist Socialism
--------------
Descendant of Chilean Presdient Aníbal Pinto, Aníbal Pinto Santa Cruz is widely know in economic circles for his written works. He had worked as a member of several economic commissions and groups based out of South America, prior to his time in Antarctica. Cruz was brought into the Chilean Antarctic Territory in part for his depth of economic knowledge, and in part to prevent Guzmán from going too far over budget during his diplomatic pursuits. After working in Antarctica for some time, Cruz would rather be elsewhere, but the government paycheck and ample free time to work in his economic theories has been pleasant, if nothing else.
--------------






 £GFX_AAC_Anibal_Pinto_Santa_Cruz_large
strings.AAC_Jose_Toribio_Merino_sec_desc:
Security Minister
Military Junta
--------------
Captain José Toribio Merino arrived in Antarctica atop the bow of his flagship, the Captain Prat, cleaving the frigid waves. He bit and clawed and bled to deliver to his fatherland its God-ordained slice of the ice during the Snipe War, saving it from the Argentine mongrels in the Battle of Greenwich Island. It was only thanks to his unshakable resolve that Chile's ambitions were not cast into the sea. And for all his sacrifice, the Hero of Snipe has been forced to grovel before limp wristed Santiago bureaucrats and crypto-Bolshevist diplomats as the commander of a mere military complement.

It is not a state of affairs Merino intends to let lie. For in the bowels of his ship, this destroyer of men has become a creator of monsters. Through the captain's dark arts, lowly marines will be turned into apex predators, instruments through which his honor will be avenged, his enemies ground into chum, and his nation will be redeemed. No matter the cost.
--------------






 £GFX_AAC_Jose_Toribio_Merino_large
strings.AAC_Luis_Danus_Covian_sec_desc:
Security Minister
Military Junta
--------------
Some may sneer and deride Luis Danús Covián as nothing more than a fawning lackey, but only a rat that knows when to abandon ship comes out unscathed. When Captain Merino steered himself into an iceberg, Covián jumped overboard, and now he sits in his former boss's chair. It's a blistering hot seat, and a man may change his allegiance but not his past. Covián, the civilian administration's loyal dog in the army, remains the same Covián who zealously joined Merino's anticommunist crusade, trained his crack marines, and supported his every machination until the very last hour. If the administration of this territory hopes to stay in calm waters, it'd be well to remember that.
--------------






 £GFX_AAC_minister_Luis_Danus_Covian_large
strings.AAC_Luis_Danus_Covian_hog_desc:
Head of Government
Military Junta
--------------
Every great leader needs a right hand man. Some may sneer and deride Luis Danús Covián as nothing more than a fawning lackey, a henchman lapping the blood off the boot of his terrible master. Covián savours the blood and finds no offense in such allegations. After all, Captain Merino would never have gotten to where he is without him.

It was Covián who molded the marine garrison into Merino's personal army of cold-hearted killers. It was Covián, from the army, who navy man Merino called for when he needed an unflinching ally in his crusade against Bolshevist conspiracy. It is Covián who Merino will rely on as he crushes the abominable Argentines. Neither would want it any other way: Covián's natural habitat in the food pyramid of his making is comfortably below the apex predator.
--------------






 £GFX_AAC_minister_Luis_Danus_Covian_large
strings.AAC_Manuel_Contreras_sec_desc:
Security Minister
Military Junta
--------------
Manuel Contreras did not quite know what his mission was when Captain Merino called up his name on Luis Covián's recommendation. Having seen the disastrous way the civilian administration had been running the Antarctic territory, he understands now. Once a star student in the same military school as Covián, he excelled in logistical planning and organization. Now his skills are put to the most difficult test, as he uncrosses the wires of the territory and refocuses it to serve one purpose and one purpose only: the achievement of Merino's plan for vengeance and reconquest.
--------------






 £GFX_AAC_minister_Manuel_Contreras_large
strings.AAC_Miguel_Serrano_for_desc:
Foreign Minister
Palingenetic Nazism
--------------
Inscrutable characters are often drawn to the Exile's horizons, but few are as enigmatic as Miguel Serrano. The orphan of a wealthy family, Serrano was quickly immersed in radical politics, once flirting with Marxism before turning sharply during the war, as he watched fascist conquests with keen interest. He joined Chile's diplomatic corps and traveled to India as part of a delegation, developing a life-long fascination with Hinduism. It was Serrano's work in the diplomatic service that brought him to Antarctica.

Few bother reading his rambling literature, let alone care to understand it. A cloud of rumors trails behind as this bizarre presence travels back and forth dark waters, representing Captain Merino's vision for Antarctica abroad. Some say he belongs more in a kooky German university, or in an insane asylum... but if his skills are useful to Merino, it seems Miguel Serrano is here to stay.
--------------






 £GFX_AAC_minister_Miguel_Serrano_large
strings.AAC_Oscar_Pinochet_eco_desc:
Economy Minister
National Conservatism
--------------
Lawyer. Historian. Poet. Explorer extraordinaire. In many ways, Óscar Pinochet resembles a legendary adventurer of Antarctica's Heroic Age. The days of Amundsen and Scott are long past now, though, and the post-Scramble battlefield belongs to diplomats who defend their nations' claims with pen and paper. If that's the role this scion of the Pinochet family has to play, then he will play it well.

The righteousness of Chile's conquest is ever-present in his mind since he first set foot in Antarctica in 1947, just before the Snipe War. Merino couldn't find someone more infatuated with the frozen continent than Pinochet. Though the latter may flinch at Merino's excesses, today the two men are brought together by their beloved fatherland's Antarctic horizon.
--------------






 £GFX_AAC_minister_Oscar_Pinochet_large

strings.AAC_Unrecognized_Antarctic_Claims_desc:
When it comes to asserting legal sovereignty over the Antarctic wastes, there is only one law that matters: might makes right. In this respect, Chile failed the most essential of tests when it was routed by Argentine forces during the Snipe War. Years of legal posturing and attempts at American mediation were shown to be as solid as new snow when the bullets started flying.

Unable to back up its claims with force of arms, the Chilean Antarctic Institute struggles to legitimize itself on the world stage. Nonetheless, her diplomats persist, working around the clock to convince the world of Chilean sovereignty in spite of the facts on the ground.
strings.AAC_Recognized_Antarctic_Claims_desc:
When it comes to asserting legal sovereignty over the Antarctic wastes, there is only one law that matters: might makes right. In this respect, Chile failed the most essential of tests when it was routed by Argentine forces during the Snipe War. Years of legal posturing and attempts at American mediation were shown to be as solid as new snow when the bullets started flying.

Now, the tireless work of its diplomats has finally borne fruit. Thanks to official recognition from the Organization of American States, Chile's voice now carries weight. Though brute force may still rule the icy wastes, the battle on the diplomatic front has been won. The Institute now holds a powerful mandate to assert its sovereignty, turning a desperate struggle for legitimacy into a confident defense of its rights.
strings.AAC_American_Backed_Antarctic_Claims_des:
When it comes to asserting legal sovereignty over the Antarctic wastes, there is only one law that matters: might makes right. In this respect, Chile failed the most essential of tests when it was routed by Argentine forces during the Snipe War. Years of legal posturing and attempts at American mediation were shown to be as solid as new snow when the bullets started flying.

Its diplomats' tireless work set the stage, but the final act was orchestrated from Washington. With a single 'gesture of goodwill', the United States secured OAS recognition of Chile's claims. On paper, it is a triumph. The Institute now holds a mandate backed by international law. But this recognition is not an earned right, but a favor granted. A debt has been incurred. Now, the Chilean flag over 'Arturo Prat' casts an eagle-winged shadow - an eternal reminder that the threads of this victory lead back to Washington.
strings.AAC_Jealous_Defence_desc: Our situation is grim. The other Antarctic Territories are large, and can afford to lose land if conflict arises. We have no such luxury. Our claims are largely unrecognized in the first place, and any loss of territory is tantamount to ceding our claim altogether. Losing this land surely means the Chilean flag will never fly in the Antarctic again. Our scouts have mapped out ideal defensive locations, and our garrisons have been trained in cold weather warfare. Should our foes strike, they will quickly learn that our claims aren't backed by paperwork alone.
strings.AAC_base_peru_desc: Our gift to the Peruvian people has become the key that opened the gates to Antarctica for them. We have let them raise their own 'Machu Picchu' at the edge of the world - a symbol of their national ambitions, built on our land and under our protection. This gesture of Pan-American brotherhood has proven wiser than any military victory. Now, when we speak on the world stage, the voice of Peru, gained through us, sounds in unison with ours. Their gratitude has become our shield, and their support - our sword in the halls where battles are fought with words.
strings.AAC_base_ecuador_desc: The fruits of President Arosemena's drunken promise have proven surprisingly sweet. The Ecuadorians, born on the equator, gaze upon Antarctica with a primal horror. Their base, Chile's 'younger brother,' requires a constant, often excessive, flow of supplies from the mainland. As experienced polar hands, the Chileans have assumed 'guardianship' over their logistics, directing and redistributing this stream. Their fear, quite unexpectedly, has filled Chilean Antarctica's own storerooms.
strings.AAC_base_cuba_desc: The revolutionary fire of the Sierra Maestra now burns with a cold flame. The fanatical zeal of the Cuban soldiers is being reforged in the icy crucible of Antarctic doctrine. The Chileans teach them not to die for an idea, but to kill for territory. This fresh blood, infused with an iron ideology, is creating a completely new type of fighter - a hybrid of a partisan and a polar wolf. Their presence unleashes Chile's own apex predators for the hunt.
strings.AAC_base_mexico_desc: Abandoned at the edge of the world, the Mexicans fulfill their unenviable role. Their presence, as a respected neutral power, transforms Chilean accusations against the Japanese whalers into cold, irrefutable facts. Every radio message from their lonely outpost is an entry in a logbook of sins, a precise coordinate marking the latest transgression of the treacherous Japanese.

strings.AAC_The_Apex_Predator_desc: The grandeur of the Great White South makes for the best conditions to hone one's physical endurance, the Chilean marines have practiced long to survive and strengthen in the frigid landscape of Antarctica they find themselves in. Slowly but surely adapting to various less conventional maneuvers and technical compromises to combat the inhospitality of the continent, perhaps one day, they may truly become like a force of nature, incomprehensible and deadly.
strings.AAC_The_Fruits_of_Diplomacy_desc:
{getaacuruguaydiplo}{getaacperudiplo}{getaacecuadordiplo}{getaacvenezueladiplo}{getaachaitidiplo}{getaaccubadiplo}{getaaccamdiplo}{getaacmexicodiplo}{getfodlinebreak}Through their whirlwind tour across the globe, Villarroel and Miranda managed to craft a landscape of diplomacy, bringing in from suppliers and sponsors luxuries to the Antarctic continent through an entangled web of commissions and favors. Trading off Chilean essentialities for various benefits has been an effective, if dangerous effort for all the individuals involved.

For now, no one can fully comprehend the potential ramifications, nor have they made themselves apparent yet.
